newsitem.title: USA: US markets greet budget pact with collective yawn.
newsitem.headline: US markets greet budget pact with collective yawn.

text.p: Disappointed by back-loaded tax increases and a dearth of structural entitlement reform, U.S. markets greeted the budget deal between Congress and the White House with a collective yawn on Tuesday.
If stock and bond markets had been more anxious about the budget deficit, they might very well have reacted negatively to the agreement, economists said.
But with a booming, low-unemployment, low-inflation economy that is balancing the budget on its own, markets took the deal, which contained few surprises, in stride.

"When you consider the details of this agreement, there is not much emphasis on cutting the growth of federal spending either near-term or longer-term," said Richard Berner, chief economist at Pittsburgh-based Mellon Bank. "Most of the emphasis is on tax cuts and providing a lot of other goodies on the spending side."
The agreement between Congressional Republicans and the Clinton administration aims to balance the $1.5 trillion budget by 2002. It would be the first balanced budget since 1969.
Both stock and bond markets had been expecting the deal since news leaked out that agreement on the broad brush strokes of a pact had been reached.

After digesting the details of the plan, announced late Monday, both bonds and stocks hovered in marginally negative territory in late morning trade, paying closer attention to employment cost data from the Labor Department.
"The budget deal has been pretty well priced into the (stock) market ... and contained very few surprises," said Alfred Kugel, senior investment strategist at Stein Roe & Farnham.
Federal Reserve Vice Chair Alice Rivlin said she doubted the agreement would have much impact on the bond market either, because the deficit was already so low.
The agreement provides for the first cut in taxes since the early years of Ronald Reagan's presidency, including a $500-per-child tax credit and a reduction in the capital gains tax.
The plan contained few pleasant surprises for the market on entitlement reform, analysts said.

Under the agreement, several health care programs would be restructured, including taking $115 billion from the Medicare program over a span of five years. But a measure which would have required wealthy senior citizens to pay higher Medicare premiums was scrapped.
The pact would raise the per-pack cigarette tax by $0.15 by the year 2002, beginning with a $0.10 hike in 2000, and extend the airline ticket tax to raise about $30 billion through 2002.

"I think it's a very wishy-washy budget deal which will make policy fiscally stimulative next year, and that is not what the economy needs," said William Dudley, chief U.S. economist at Goldman Sachs & Co.

Dudley said the tax increases had been back-loaded and noted that the combination of child tax credits, education aid and two-stage capital gains tax reduction would make the tax code more complicated, resulting in real costs to the economy.
Republicans won provisions including a cut in the capital gains tax rate to 20 percent from 28 percent, and a second drop to 18 percent in 2001 for long-term holdings.
Gail Dudack, chief investment strategist at UBS Securities, was more sanguine about the cut in the capital gains tax, predicting longer-term benefits to the stock market.

"When we have a significant change in the capital gains tax, it is initially negative for markets as it allows a lot of people to lock in profits," she said. "But over the long run, it is good for stocks and investments."
